senses.gloss:
candana
(‘that which gives joy’)
------------------------------------------
Candana is sandalwood (Santalum album) well-known for its fragrance and medicinal properties. Indians knew its use even from very ancient days.
It grows mostly in the Malayagiri (Western Ghats). Three varieties—white, yellow and red—are known to exist. Because of its fragrance and cooling properties it is used as an item of luxury and also for its curative effects. Its paste is one of the most important items offered to a deity in ritualistic worship and is called ‘gandha’. In some temples, on certain special days, the image of the deity is decorated entirely with sandal paste.

Candravaṁśa
(‘dynasty or race of चन्द्र’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu itihāsas and पुराणस् contain lots of historical material. Two dynasties, the Sūryavaṁśa and the चन्द्रवṁश (Solar and Lunar dynasties) have often been mentioned in these works.
Candravaṁśa starts with चन्द्र-सोम. His son was बुध from Iḷā, and was better known as Purūrava Aila. He became so famous and important that the Lunar dynasty is often stated to have commenced from him. He ruled from Pratiṣṭhāna (now a village Pihan by name, near Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh). नहुष, ययाति and पूरु are the other celebrated rulers in this dynasty. The dynasty branched off with यदु, the eldest son of ययाति, into the Yādava dynasty, of which बलराम and Śrī कृष्ण were the most famous descendants.
Pūru’s descendants came to be known as Pauravas. The Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas belonged to this line.
Ānavas and Haihayas were the other branches of the lunar race.

candragrahaṇa
(‘seizing of the मोओन्’)
------------------------------------------
See GRAHAṆA.

Candra
(‘one who delights or shines’)
------------------------------------------
The deity who presides over the मोओन् is called ‘Soma,’ ‘Indu’ or ‘Candra’. The entire ninth मण्डल of the ऋग्वेद is devoted to his praise. He is the presiding deity of the सोम creeper, the juice of which is often used in sacrifices as oblation and also partaken by the participants. Sometimes identified with the Supreme God, he is said to cure the mortals of their diseases and lead them to immortal blissful worlds. He rules over the मिन्द् and activates our speech. Hence he is sometimes called ‘Vācaspati’ or the ‘Lord of speech’.
The पुरुषसूक्त of the ऋग्वेद declares that चन्द्र was born out of the मिन्द् of the Supreme Being.
In the mythological literature, his birth is described variously as the embodiment of the brilliant light that emerged from the eyes of the sage अत्रि, as the son of धर्म-प्रजापति or as rising out of the ocean of milk when it was being churned. शिव wore him as his diadem. The 27 constellations of स्तर्स् like रोहिणी are described as his wives. His waxing and waning are due to a curse he got from his ड़थेर्-in-law, दक्ष. His एच्लिप्से is due to his being swallowed by the demon राहु. He has special power over the vegetation on this earth. He is full of अमृत or nectar. That is why the gods drink him. He is replenished by the offerings in the sacrifices. He is the originator of the चन्द्रवṁश or the Lunar dynasty of which Śrī कृष्ण was the last member.
Works on Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् consider him as one of the नवग्रहस् or nine प्लनेत्स्, with a beneficial influence.
Iconographically, he is represented with a face and two hands holding lotuses, sitting in a chariot of two or three wheels and drawn by ten horses.
In the works on योग and तन्त्रस्, चन्द्र is described as the ‘moon of mystery,’ full of nectar, existing just below the middle of the सहस्रार. By contemplating on him the योगि becomes fit to be adored by the world.
Connection between the phases of the मोओन् and the condition of mental patients has long been recognized by the Hindu works on health and sickness.

cāndrāyaṇa
(‘[following] the phases of the मोओन्’)
------------------------------------------
The धर्मशास्त्रस् have described several kinds of prāyaścittas or expiations for sins of omission and commission. चान्द्रायण is a universal expiation prescribed for almost any sin, especially where no other specific remedy has been suggested.
The name is derived from the fact that in this expiation, the eating pattern follows the phases of the मोओन्. Starting with 15 morsels of ड़ोओद् (per day) on the full-मोओन्, the same is gradually reduced by one morsel every day, ending in total ड़स्तिन्ग् on the new-मोओन् day. It is again increased, now from 1 to 15 morsels, till the full-मोओन् day. This is one cycle. It can be repeated as many times as desired or needed. Since the quantity of ड़ोओद् is full in the beginning and end, becoming nil at the middle, it is called ‘pipīlikāmadhya’ or ‘middle of an ant.’
If on the other hand, it is started with one morsel on the first day after the new-मोओन्, increasing to 15 morsels on the full-मोओन् and again reducing to nil on the new-मोओन्, it is called ‘yavamadhya’ or ‘middle of the wheat grain.’ The similes are self-explanatory. Size of the morsel is that of a big myrobalan fruit.
Prescribing 8 morsels of ड़ोओद् per day and keeping the month as a unit period, other varieties of चान्द्रायण as यति-चान्द्रायण have been derived by permutations of the morsels.
Tonsure of hair, initial ड़स्तिन्ग्, offering libations of water and clarified butter, consecrating the sacrificial ड़ोओद् and worship of moon—these are common disciplines for all the candrāyaṇas.
See also ARDHAKṚCCHRA, KṚCCHRA and PRĀYAŚCITTA.

Candrabhāgā
( ‘[the place] where चन्द्र was divided’)
------------------------------------------
Once there was a dispute about चन्द्र (moon) between शिव who had worn him as his diadem and the nakṣatras (constellations) who were his wives. ब्रह्मा mediated, divided चन्द्र into two halves and distributed them to the disputants. The place in the हिमालयस् where this was done came to be known as ‘Candrabhāgā.’ A river arose at that spot and it was also christened ‘Candra-bhāgā.’ This is the story given in the महाभारत.
Actually the river rises in the हिमालयस् in two streams, one being called Candrā and the other, Bhāgā. The two join at Taṇḍi and the united stream is known as चन्द्रभागा. It is identified with the river Chenab now in Pakistan. It is called ‘Asiknī’ in the ऋग्वेद.
Sāmba, the son of Śrī कृष्ण, is said to have built a temple for सूर्य (sun) at the spot where it joins the river Sindhū (Indus).
There is another small river of the same name in Orissa. At the place where it joins the bay of Bengal, the famous सूर्य temple of कोणार्क (Konarak) has been built.
The river Bhīmā, a tributary of the Kṛṣṇā, in Maharashtra is also known as चन्द्रभागा. The celebrated Viṭhoba temple is situated very near this river.

candrikā
(‘moonlight’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘candrikā’ which literally means moonlight, has often been used in a figurative sense to any literary work that throws a ‘cool light’ on any subject. Two such works that are comparatively more well-known are the चन्द्रिका of Jñānottama and the चन्द्रिका of व्यासतीर्थ.
The former is a commentary on the नैष्कर्म्य Siddhi of सुरेश्वर (8th cent. A.D.), a disciple of शङ्कर, by one Jñānottama, who was probably a pontiff of the Advaita-मठ at काञ्चीपुरम्, and lived around A.D. 1300.
The latter is actually an abbreviation for Tātparyacandrikā, a commentary by व्यासतीर्थ (A.D. 1447-1539) on the Tattva-prakāśikā of जयतीर्थ (14th cent. A.D.), this again being a commentary on मध्वाचार्य’s (A. D. 1238-1317) Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya.
